claim: KvS proteins are voltage-gated potassium channel subunits that form functional channels when assembled into heteromers with Kv2.1 (KCNB1) or Kv2.2 (KCNB2).
source: KvS proteins are voltage-gated potassium channel subunits that form functional channels when assembled into heteromers with Kv2.1 (KCNB1) or Kv2.2 (KCNB2).
evidence: This is a foundational statement about KvS proteins supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mammals have 10 KvS subunits: Kv5.1 (KCNF1), Kv6.1 (KCNG1), Kv6.2 (KCNG2), Kv6.3 (KCNG3), Kv6.4 (KCNG4), Kv8.1 (KCNV1), Kv8.2 (KCNV2), Kv9.1 (KCNS1), Kv9.2 (KCNS2), and Kv9.3 (KCNS3).
source: Mammals have 10 KvS subunits: Kv5.1 (KCNF1), Kv6.1 (KCNG1), Kv6.2 (KCNG2), Kv6.3 (KCNG3), Kv6.4 (KCNG4), Kv8.1 (KCNV1), Kv8.2 (KCNV2), Kv9.1 (KCNS1), Kv9.2 (KCNS2), and Kv9.3 (KCNS3).
evidence: This is a factual enumeration of mammalian KvS subunits based on established nomenclature and knowledge.

claim: Electrically excitable cells broadly express channels containing Kv2 subunits and most neurons have substantial Kv2 conductance.
source: Electrically excitable cells broadly express channels containing Kv2 subunits and most neurons have substantial Kv2 conductance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the Introduction section referencing prior literature.

claim: Two potent Kv2 inhibitors, RY785 and guangxitoxin-1E (GxTX), used in combination, can distinguish conductances of Kv2/KvS heteromers and Kv2-only channels.
source: Here, we identify that two potent Kv2 inhibitors, used in combination, can distinguish conductances of Kv2/KvS heteromers and Kv2-only channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-5.

claim: Kv5, Kv6, Kv8, or Kv9-containing channels are resistant to the Kv2-selective pore-blocker RY785 yet remain sensitive to the Kv2-selective voltage sensor modulator guangxitoxin-1E (GxTX).
source: We find that Kv5, Kv6, Kv8, or Kv9-containing channels are resistant to the Kv2-selective pore-blocker RY785 yet remain sensitive to the Kv2-selective voltage sensor modulator guangxitoxin-1E (GxTX).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: In mouse superior cervical ganglion neurons, predominantly RY785-sensitive conductances consistent with channels composed entirely of Kv2 subunits are found.
source: Using these inhibitors in mouse superior cervical ganglion neurons, we find predominantly RY785-sensitive conductances consistent with channels composed entirely of Kv2 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: In mouse and human dorsal root ganglion neurons, RY785-resistant but GxTX-sensitive conductances consistent with Kv2/KvS heteromeric channels predominate.
source: In contrast, RY785-resistant but GxTX-sensitive conductances consistent with Kv2/KvS heteromeric channels predominate in mouse and human dorsal root ganglion neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Kv2 channels have profound impacts on vision, seizure suppression, stroke recovery, pain signaling, blood pressure, insulin secretion, and reproduction.
source: Consistent with this widespread expression, Kv2 channels have profound impacts on many aspects of our physiology including vision, seizure suppression, stroke recovery, pain signaling, blood pressure, insulin secretion, and reproduction (Bocksteins, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bocksteins, 2016.

claim: KvS subunits are an understudied class of voltage-gated K+ channel subunits that comprise one fourth of mammalian Kv subunit types.
source: KvS subunits are an understudied class of voltage-gated K+ channel (Kv) subunits that comprise one fourth of mammalian Kv subunit types.
evidence: This is a factual statement based on the enumeration of KvS subunits relative to total Kv subunits.

claim: KvS alpha subunits co-assemble with Kv2 alpha subunits to form heterotetrameric Kv2/KvS channels in which the KvS subunit makes up part of the K+-conductive pathway.
source: Rather, KvS alpha subunits co-assemble with Kv2 alpha subunits to form heterotetrameric Kv2/KvS channels in which the KvS subunit makes up part of the K+-conductive pathway (Salinas et al., 1997b; Kramer et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Salinas et al., 1997b and Kramer et al., 1998.

claim: Kv2/KvS heteromers have biophysical properties distinct from those of homomeric Kv2 channels.
source: Kv2/KvS heteromers have biophysical properties distinct from those of homomeric Kv2 channels (Post et al., 1996; Salinas et al., 1997a; Kramer et al., 1998; Richardson and Kaczmarek, 2000; Zhong et al., 2010; Bocksteins et al., 2012; Bocksteins et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: KvS mRNAs are expressed in tissue and cell-specific manners that overlap with Kv2.1 or Kv2.2 expression.
source: KvS mRNAs are expressed in tissue and cell-specific manners that overlap with Kv2.1 or Kv2.2 expression (Castellano et al., 1997; Salinas et al., 1997a; Kramer et al., 1998; Bocksteins et al., 2012; Bocksteins and Snyders, 2012; Bocksteins, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Genetic mutations and gene-targeting studies have linked disruptions in the function of different KvS subunits to retinal cone dystrophy, male infertility, seizures, and changes in pain sensitivity.
source: Consistent with narrow expression of the many KvS subunits, genetic mutations and gene-targeting studies have linked disruptions in the function of different KvS subunits to defects in distinct organ systems including retinal cone dystrophy (Wu et al., 2006; Hart et al., 2019; Inamdar et al., 2022), male infertility (Regnier et al., 2017), seizures (Jorge et al., 2011), and changes in pain sensitivity (Tsantoulas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies of the physiological roles of KvS subunits have been hindered by a lack of tools to identify native KvS conductances.
source: However, studies of the physiological roles of KvS subunits have been hindered by a lack of tools to identify native KvS conductances.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by the lack of prior pharmacological tools discussed in the manuscript.

claim: No drugs are known to be selective for KvS subunits.
source: No drugs are known to be selective for KvS subunits.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of pharmacological tools in the field.

claim: Guangxitoxin-1E (GxTX) has remarkable specificity for Kv2 channel subunits over other voltage-gated channels.
source: An exemplar of this class is the tarantula toxin guangxitoxin-1E (GxTX), which has remarkable specificity for Kv2 channel subunits over other voltage-gated channels (Herrington et al., 2006; Thapa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Herrington et al., 2006 and Thapa et al., 2021.

claim: GxTX binds to the voltage sensor of each Kv2 subunit and stabilizes that voltage sensor in a resting state to prevent channel opening.
source: GxTX binds to the voltage sensor of each Kv2 subunit (Milescu et al., 2009), and stabilizes that voltage sensor in a resting state to prevent channel opening (Tilley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Milescu et al., 2009 and Tilley et al., 2019.

claim: GxTX binding requires a specific sequence of residues, TIFLTES, at the extracellular end of the Kv2 subunit S3 transmembrane helix.
source: GxTX binding requires a specific sequence of residues, TIFLTES, at the extracellular end of the Kv2 subunit S3 transmembrane helix (Milescu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Milescu et al., 2013.

claim: The GxTX-binding sequence is conserved between Kv2 channels but is not retained by any KvS subunit.
source: This GxTX-binding sequence is conserved between Kv2 channels but is not retained by any KvS subunit.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence conservation that can be inferred from sequence analysis.

claim: RY785 is the most selective for Kv2 channels over other channel types among a family of small molecules discovered in a high throughput screen for use-dependent Kv2 inhibitors.
source: A second class of selective Kv2 inhibitors is a family of small molecules discovered in a high throughput screen for use-dependent Kv2 inhibitors (Herrington et al., 2011). Of these, RY785 is the most selective for Kv2 channels over other channel types.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herrington et al., 2011.

claim: RY785 acts like a pore blocker which binds in the central cavity of Kv2 channels.
source: RY785 acts like a pore blocker which binds in the central cavity of Kv2 channels (Marquis and Sack, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marquis and Sack, 2022.

claim: The central cavity-lining residues of all KvS subunits have differences from Kv2 subunits.
source: The central cavity-lining residues of all KvS subunits have differences from Kv2 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Coexpression of Kv5.1 with Kv2.1 led to a conductance that was resistant to RY785.
source: We recently reported that coexpression of Kv5.1 with Kv2.1 led to a conductance that was resistant to RY785 (Ferns et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferns et al., 2025.

claim: After transfection of Kv8.1 into Kv2.1-CHO cells, a sizable component of the delayed rectifier current became resistant to 1 μM RY785.
source: After transfection of Kv8.1 into Kv2.1-CHO cells, we find that a sizable component of the delayed rectifier current became resistant to 1 μM RY785 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The RY785-resistant current in Kv8.1-transfected Kv2.1-CHO cells was inhibited by 100 nM GxTX.
source: This RY785-resistant current was inhibited by 100 nM GxTX, suggesting that the GxTX-sensitivity arises from inclusion of Kv2.1 subunits in the channels underlying the RY785-resistant current.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In Kv2.1-CHO cells transfected with Navβ2, 1 μM RY785 efficiently blocked Kv2.1 conductance, leaving 4 ± 0.6% (mean ± SEM) of current.
source: In Kv2.1-CHO cells transfected with Navβ2, 1 μM RY785 efficiently blocked Kv2.1 conductance, leaving 4 ± 0.6% (mean ± SEM) of current (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and D.

claim: In Kv2.1-CHO cells transfected with AMIGO1, 1 μM RY785 blocked Kv2.1 conductances, leaving 0.6 ± 1% (SEM) of current.
source: 1 μM RY785 blocked Kv2.1 conductances in cells transfected with AMIGO1, leaving 0.6 ± 1% (SEM) of current (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Currents resistant to 0.35 μM RY785 in Kv8.1-transfected cells were blocked by higher concentrations of RY785, with nearly complete block observed in 35 μM RY785.
source: Notably, currents resistant to 0.35 μM RY785 were blocked by higher concentrations of RY785, with nearly complete block observed in 35 μM RY785 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The IC50 of RY785 for Kv2.1/Kv8.1 heteromers is 5±1 μM (SD).
source: This protocol revealed an IC50 of 5±1 μM (SD; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Hill coefficient of RY785 block of Kv2.1/Kv8.1 is 1.2±0.2, consistent with 1:1 binding to a homogenous population of RY785-inhibited channels.
source: The Hill coefficient of 1.2±0.2 is consistent with 1:1 binding to a homogenous population of RY785-inhibited channels.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of concentration-effect data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Kv2.1/Kv8.1 currents were unblocked in the first current test following RY785 washout.
source: Kv2.1/Kv8.1 currents were unblocked in the first current test following RY785 washout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RY785 becomes trapped in deactivated Kv2.1 homomers and unblocks much more slowly, with a time constant of about 2 hr at –92 mV or 100 s at +28 mV.
source: This is distinct from Kv2.1 homomers, where RY785 becomes trapped in deactivated channels and unblocks much more slowly, with a time constant of about 2 hr at –92 mV or 100 s at +28 mV (Marquis and Sack, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marquis and Sack, 2022.

claim: Kv8.1-containing channels in Kv2.1-CHO cells form a pharmacologically homogenous population with an affinity for RY785 ~3 orders of magnitude weaker than Kv2.1 homomers.
source: Overall, the results suggest that Kv8.1-containing channels in these Kv2.1-CHO cells form a pharmacologically homogenous population with an affinity for RY785 ~3 orders of magnitude weaker than Kv2.1 homomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IC50 values measured for Kv2.1 homomers (~6 nM) and Kv2.1/Kv8.1 heteromers (~5 μM).

claim: Cells transfected with Kv8.1 and blocked with 1 μM RY785 had a significantly slower activation time constant and lower sigmoidicity than those only expressing Kv2.1.
source: Cells transfected with Kv8.1 and blocked with 1 μM RY785 had a significantly slower activation time constant and lower sigmoidicity (shorter relative activation delay) than those only expressing Kv2.1 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The half-maximal conductance of Kv8.1-transfected cells is shifted positive relative to Kv2.1 alone.
source: Conductance-voltage relations were fit with a Boltzmann function (equation 2) revealing that the half-maximal conductance of Kv8.1-transfected cells is shifted positive relative to Kv2.1 alone (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Currents from Kv8.1-transfected cells inactivated less during a 10 s step to –9 mV.
source: Currents from Kv8.1-transfected cells inactivated less during a 10 s step to –9 mV (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The steady-state inactivation of Kv8.1-transfected cells was shifted to more negative voltages and is less steep than Kv2.1-transfected cells.
source: However, the steady-state inactivation of Kv8.1-transfected cells was shifted to more negative voltages and is less steep than Kv2.1-transfected cells (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I–K.

claim: The biophysical properties of RY785-resistant currents in cells transfected with Kv8.1 are consistent with prior reports of Kv8.1/Kv2 biophysics.
source: Overall, the biophysical properties reported here are consistent with a previous report which identified that co-expression of Kv8.1 with Kv2.1 in Xenopus oocytes slows the rate of activation, reduces inactivation and shifts steady-state inactivation to more negative voltages (Salinas et al., 1997a).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current study's data with prior literature (Salinas et al., 1997a).

claim: In 1 μM RY785, >10% of the voltage-gated current remained in 12/13 Kv5.1, 9/14 Kv6.4, and 5/5 Kv9.3 transfected cells.
source: We observed that, in 1 μM RY785,>10% of the voltage-gated current remained in 12/13 Kv5.1, 9/14 Kv6.4, and 5/5 Kv9.3 transfected cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Addition of 100 nM GxTX blocked RY785-resistant current from cells transfected with Kv5.1, Kv6.4, and Kv9.3.
source: Addition of 100 nM GxTX blocked RY785-resistant current from cells transfected with each of these KvS subunits.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: Immunofluorescence for Kv5.1, Kv9.3, and Kv2.1 appeared localized to the perimeter of transfected Kv2.1-CHO cells.
source: While a fraction of KvS subunits appear to be retained intracellularly, immunofluorescence for Kv5.1, Kv9.3, and Kv2.1 also appeared localized to the perimeter of transfected Kv2.1-CHO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Voltage-gated outward currents in cells transfected with members from each KvS subtype have decreased sensitivity to RY785 but remain sensitive to GxTX.
source: These results show that voltage-gated outward currents in cells transfected with members from each KvS subtype have decreased sensitivity to RY785 but remain sensitive to GxTX.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Rat superior cervical ganglion (SCG) neurons have robust GxTX-sensitive conductances.
source: Rat superior cervical ganglion (SCG) neurons have robust GxTX-sensitive conductances (Liu and Bean, 2014) yet transcriptomics have revealed little evidence of KvS expression (Sapio et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu and Bean, 2014 and Sapio et al., 2020.

claim: Transcriptomics have revealed little evidence of KvS expression in rat superior cervical ganglion neurons.
source: Rat superior cervical ganglion (SCG) neurons have robust GxTX-sensitive conductances (Liu and Bean, 2014) yet transcriptomics have revealed little evidence of KvS expression (Sapio et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sapio et al., 2020.

claim: Exposing SCG neurons to 1 μM RY785 inhibited most of the voltage-gated current, and subsequent addition of 100 nM GxTX to the same neurons inhibited little additional current.
source: We found that exposing SCG neurons to 1 μM RY785 inhibited most of the voltage-gated current, and subsequent addition of 100 nM GxTX to the same neurons inhibited little additional current (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Tail currents after application of 1 μM RY785 were decreased by 88 ± 5% (mean ± SEM) in SCG neurons.
source: Tail currents after application of 1 μM RY785 were decreased by 88 ± 5% (mean ± SEM) in SCG neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Current activation in SCG neurons began to be apparent at –45 mV and had a conductance that was half maximal at –11 mV.
source: Current activation began to be apparent at –45 mV and had a conductance that was half maximal at –11 mV (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The faster component of deactivation of Kv2-like currents in SCG neurons had a time constant of 16ms±0.6 (mean ± SEM) at –45 mV.
source: The faster component of deactivation of Kv2-like currents in SCG neurons had a time constant of 16ms±0.6 (mean ± SEM) at –45 mV (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 1 µM RY785 almost completely inhibits endogenous Kv2-like conductances in mouse SCG neurons, consistent with mouse SCG neurons having few, if any, functional Kv2/KvS heteromers.
source: Together these results show that 1 µM RY785 almost completely inhibits endogenous Kv2-like conductances in these mouse neurons, consistent with mouse SCG neurons having few, if any, functional Kv2/KvS heteromers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) somatosensory neurons express Kv2 proteins.
source: Mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) somatosensory neurons express Kv2 proteins (Stewart et al., 2024), have GxTX-sensitive conductances (Zheng et al., 2019), and express a variety of KvS transcripts (Bocksteins et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2019), yet transcript abundance does not necessarily correlate with functional protein abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stewart et al., 2024.

claim: Mouse DRG neurons have GxTX-sensitive conductances.
source: Mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) somatosensory neurons express Kv2 proteins (Stewart et al., 2024), have GxTX-sensitive conductances (Zheng et al., 2019), and express a variety of KvS transcripts (Bocksteins et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2019), yet transcript abundance does not necessarily correlate with functional protein abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2019.

claim: Mouse DRG neurons express a variety of KvS transcripts.
source: Mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) somatosensory neurons express Kv2 proteins (Stewart et al., 2024), have GxTX-sensitive conductances (Zheng et al., 2019), and express a variety of KvS transcripts (Bocksteins et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2019), yet transcript abundance does not necessarily correlate with functional protein abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bocksteins et al., 2009 and Zheng et al., 2019.

claim: Deep sequencing identified that mRNA transcripts for Kcnf1 (Kv5.1), Kcng2 (Kv6.2), Kcng3 (Kv6.3), and Kcns1 (Kv9.1) are present in GFP+ neurons of MrgprdGFP mice.
source: Deep sequencing identified that mRNA transcripts for Kcnf1 (Kv5.1), Kcng2 (Kv6.2), Kcng3 (Kv6.3), and Kcns1 (Kv9.1) are present in GFP+ neurons of this mouse line (Zheng et al., 2019) and we confirmed the presence of Kcnf1 (Kv5.1) and Kcns1 (Kv9.1) transcripts in GFP+ neurons from MrgprdGFP mice using RNAscope (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2019 and confirmed by RNAscope data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Application of 1 μM RY785 inhibited outward currents in GFP+ neurons from MrgprdGFP mice, but a prominent delayed-rectifier outward conductance with slow deactivation remained.
source: Application of 1 μM RY785 inhibited outward currents somewhat, but unlike in SCG neurons, a prominent delayed-rectifier outward conductance with slow deactivation remained (Figure 7A left panel).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Tail currents in 1 μM RY785 decreased 29 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) in GFP+ neurons from MrgprdGFP mice.
source: Tail currents in 1 μM RY785 decreased 29 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) (Figure 7B left panel).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Subsequent application of 100 nM GxTX decreased tail currents by 68 ± 5% (mean ± SEM) of their original amplitude before RY785 in GFP+ neurons from MrgprdGFP mice.
source: Subsequent application of 100 nM GxTX decreased tail currents by 68 ± 5% (mean ± SEM) of their original amplitude before RY785.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, 58 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) of the delayed rectifier conductance was resistant to RY785 yet sensitive to GxTX (KvS-like) in GFP+ neurons from MrgprdGFP mice.
source: Under these conditions, 58 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) of the delayed rectifier conductance was resistant to RY785 yet sensitive to GxTX (KvS-like; Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The KvS-like currents in GFP+ neurons from MrgprdGFP mice deactivated slower than Kv2-like currents.
source: We did note that the KvS-like currents deactivated slower than Kv2-like currents (Figure 7E), consistent with the effects of several KvS subunits whose transcripts are expressed in nociceptor DRG neurons.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In GFP+ neurons from CalcaGFP mice, a fraction of outward current was inhibited by 1 µM RY785 and additional current inhibited by 100 nM GxTX.
source: In GFP+ neurons from CalcaGFP mice, we found that a fraction of outward current was inhibited by 1 µM RY785 and additional current inhibited by 100 nM GxTX (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A-C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: In CalcaGFP neurons, 58 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) was KvS-like.
source: In these experiments, 58 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) was KvS-like (Figure 7—figure supplement 3D) identifying that KvS-like conductances are present in these peptidergic nociceptors.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Human DRG neurons express Kv2 proteins.
source: Human DRG neurons express Kv2 proteins (Stewart et al., 2024), and express KvS transcripts (Ray et al., 2018) suggesting that they may have Kv2/KvS conductances.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stewart et al., 2024.

claim: Human DRG neurons express KvS transcripts.
source: Human DRG neurons express Kv2 proteins (Stewart et al., 2024), and express KvS transcripts (Ray et al., 2018) suggesting that they may have Kv2/KvS conductances.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ray et al., 2018.

claim: In human DRG neurons, a fraction of outward current was inhibited by 1 µM RY785 and additional current was inhibited by 100 nM GxTX, consistent with the presence of KvS-like conductances.
source: In human DRG neurons, a fraction of outward current was inhibited by 1 µM RY785 and additional current was inhibited by 100 nM GxTX, consistent with the presence of KvS-like conductances (Figure 8A, B and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A, B and C.

claim: Of the total conductance sensitive to RY785 +GxTX in human DRG neurons, 76 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) was KvS-like.
source: Of the total conductance sensitive to RY785 +GxTX in these human DRG neurons, 76 ± 2% (mean ± SEM) was KvS-like (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Human DRG neurons can produce endogenous voltage-gated currents with pharmacology and gating consistent with Kv2/KvS heteromeric channels.
source: Overall, these results show that human DRG neurons can produce endogenous voltage-gated currents with pharmacology and gating consistent with Kv2/KvS heteromeric channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The combination of GxTX and RY785 can distinguish conductances of Kv2-only channels from channels that contain the KvS subtypes, Kv5, Kv6, Kv8, or Kv9.
source: We identify that the combination of GxTX and RY785 can distinguish conductances of Kv2-only channels from channels that contain the KvS subtypes, Kv5, Kv6, Kv8, or Kv9.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data in Figures 1-8.

claim: RY785 blocks homomeric Kv2 channels, and subsequent application of GxTX selectively inhibits Kv2/KvS heteromeric channels.
source: RY785 blocks homomeric Kv2 channels, and subsequent application of GxTX selectively inhibits Kv2/KvS heteromeric channels.
evidence: This is a summary of the pharmacological strategy supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: It is remarkable that resistance to RY785 is shared across all of the KvS subtypes.
source: It is remarkable that resistance to RY785 is shared across all of the KvS subtypes.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the experimental findings shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Kv2.1/Kv8.1 conductances are ~1000 times less sensitive to RY785 than Kv2.1 homomer conductances in the same cell line.
source: We found Kv2.1/Kv8.1 conductances to be ~1000 times less sensitive to RY785 than Kv2.1 homomer conductances in the same cell line.
evidence: This is based on comparison of IC50 values: ~6 nM for Kv2.1 homomers vs ~5 μM for Kv2.1/Kv8.1 heteromers.

claim: The top-scoring docking pose has RY785 positioned below the selectivity filter and off-axis of the pore in a Kv2.1 homomer model.
source: The top-scoring docking pose has RY785 positioned below the selectivity filter and off-axis of the pore (Figure 9A), similar to a stable pose observed in molecular dynamics simulations (Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 9A and supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2024.

claim: In the top-scoring docking pose, RY785 contacts a collection of Kv2.1 residues that vary in every KvS subtype.
source: In this pose, RY785 contacts a collection of Kv2.1 residues that vary in every KvS subtype (Figure 9B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling and sequence analysis shown in Figure 9B, D and E.

claim: RY785 bound similarly to a 3:1 model of Kv2.1/Kv8.1, in contact with the three Kv2.1 subunits, yet avoided the Kv8.1 subunit.
source: Notably, RY785 bound similarly to a 3:1 model of Kv2.1/Kv8.1, in contact with the three Kv2.1 subunits, yet avoided the Kv8.1 subunit (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The structural modeling suggests that KvS subunits sterically interfere with RY785 binding to the central cavity.
source: Overall, the structural modeling suggests that KvS subunits sterically interfere with RY785 binding to the central cavity, while functional data suggest KvS subunits disrupt RY785 trapping in closed states.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on computational modeling shown in Figure 9.

claim: Functional data suggest KvS subunits disrupt RY785 trapping in closed states.
source: Overall, the structural modeling suggests that KvS subunits sterically interfere with RY785 binding to the central cavity, while functional data suggest KvS subunits disrupt RY785 trapping in closed states.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on functional data showing rapid recovery of Kv2.1/Kv8.1 currents following RY785 washout.

claim: While Kv2 subunits are broadly expressed in electrically excitable cells throughout the brain and body, transcripts for KvS subunits have unique expression patterns that are specific to each KvS subtype.
source: While Kv2 subunits are broadly expressed in electrically excitable cells throughout the brain and body, transcripts for KvS subunits have unique expression patterns that are specific to each KvS subtype (Bocksteins, 2016) and can fluctuate with age (Regnier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bocksteins, 2016 and Regnier et al., 2016.

claim: Native Kv2 channels in mouse brain contain KvS subunit proteins, including Kv5.1, Kv8.1, Kv9.1, and Kv9.2.
source: We found recently that native Kv2 channels in mouse brain contain KvS subunit proteins, including Kv5.1, Kv8.1, Kv9.1, and Kv9.2.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferns et al., 2025.

claim: The KvS mass spectral abundance relative to Kv2.1 in mouse brain ranged from ≈18% for Kv5.1–2% for Kv9.1.
source: Notably, the KvS mass spectral abundance relative to Kv2.1 ranged from ≈18% for Kv5.1–2% for Kv9.1 (Ferns et al., 2025), and Kv5.1 protein expression was largely restricted to cortical neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferns et al., 2025.

claim: Kv5.1 protein expression in mouse brain was largely restricted to cortical neurons.
source: Notably, the KvS mass spectral abundance relative to Kv2.1 ranged from ≈18% for Kv5.1–2% for Kv9.1 (Ferns et al., 2025), and Kv5.1 protein expression was largely restricted to cortical neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferns et al., 2025.

claim: Genetic mutations and gene targeting studies have linked disruptions in the function of KvS-containing channels to epilepsy, neuropathic pain sensitivity, labor pain and retinal cone dystrophy.
source: Genetic mutations and gene targeting studies have linked disruptions in the function of KvS-containing channels to epilepsy (Jorge et al., 2011), neuropathic pain sensitivity (Tsantoulas et al., 2018), labor pain (Lee et al., 2020) and retinal cone dystrophy (Wu et al., 2006; Hart et al., 2019; Inamdar et al., 2022), stressing their functional importance in specific cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The unique pharmacology of KvS-containing channels identified here provides a new and direct method of identifying conductances mediated by KvS-containing channels in native neurons.
source: The unique pharmacology of KvS-containing channels identified here provides a new and direct method of identifying conductances mediated by KvS-containing channels in native neurons and establishing what contributions KvS subunits make to electrophysiological signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: KvS transcripts show far greater tissue- and cell-type specific expression relative to Kv2.
source: KvS transcripts show far greater tissue- and cell-type specific expression relative to Kv2 (Bishop et al., 2015; Bocksteins, 2016), and we identified prominent Kv2 conductances with KvS-like pharmacology in mouse nociceptor and human DRG neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bishop et al., 2015 and Bocksteins, 2016.

claim: KvS-targeted drugs could offer greater specificity and the ability to modulate neuronal excitability in a variety of pathological contexts, such as neuropathic pain.
source: Consequently, KvS-targeted drugs could offer greater specificity and the ability to modulate neuronal excitability in a variety of pathological contexts, such as neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings of the study.

claim: 1 μM RY785 or 100 nM GxTX blocked almost all the voltage-gated K+ conductance of the Kv2.1-CHO cell line, with 1±2% or 0 ± 0.1% (mean ± SEM) current remaining respectively at 0 mV.
source: We previously found that 1 μM RY785 or 100 nM GxTX blocked almost all the voltage-gated K+ conductance of this Kv2.1-CHO cell line, with 1±2% or 0 ± 0.1% (mean ± SEM) current remaining respectively at 0 mV (Tilley et al., 2019; Marquis and Sack, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tilley et al., 2019 and Marquis and Sack, 2022.

claim: Co-expression of KvS and Kv2 subunits can result in Kv2 homomers and Kv2/KvS heteromers.
source: Co-expression of KvS and Kv2 subunits can result in Kv2 homomers and Kv2/KvS heteromers (Pisupati et al., 2018), and we presume variability in the RY785-sensitive fraction results from cell-to-cell variability in the proportion of Kv8.1-containing channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pisupati et al., 2018.

claim: AMIGO1 promotes voltage sensor activation of Kv2.1 channels in Kv2.1-CHO cells.
source: AMIGO1 promotes voltage sensor activation of Kv2.1 channels in these Kv2.1-CHO cells (Sepela et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sepela et al., 2022.

claim: Concentrations of RY785 that partially block Kv2.1/Kv8.1 modified the kinetics of voltage-dependent gating, suggesting state-dependent block.
source: While concentrations of RY785 that partially block Kv2.1/Kv8.1 modified the kinetics of voltage-dependent gating, suggesting state-dependent block, we did not observe modification of kinetics with 3.5 μM or lower concentrations of RY785 (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Co-expression of Kv8.1 with Kv2.1 in Xenopus oocytes slows the rate of activation, reduces inactivation and shifts steady-state inactivation to more negative voltages.
source: Overall, the biophysical properties reported here are consistent with a previous report which identified that co-expression of Kv8.1 with Kv2.1 in Xenopus oocytes slows the rate of activation, reduces inactivation and shifts steady-state inactivation to more negative voltages (Salinas et al., 1997a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salinas et al., 1997a.

claim: Kv5.1/Kv2.1 heteromers play an important role in controlling the excitability of mouse urinary bladder smooth muscle.
source: Kv5.1/Kv2.1 heteromers play an important role in controlling the excitability of mouse urinary bladder smooth muscle (Malysz and Petkov, 2020), mutations in Kv6.4 have been shown to influence human labor pain (Lee et al., 2020), and deficiency of Kv9.3 disrupts parvalbumin interneuron physiology in mouse prefrontal cortex (Miyamae et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Malysz and Petkov, 2020.

claim: Mutations in Kv6.4 have been shown to influence human labor pain.
source: Kv5.1/Kv2.1 heteromers play an important role in controlling the excitability of mouse urinary bladder smooth muscle (Malysz and Petkov, 2020), mutations in Kv6.4 have been shown to influence human labor pain (Lee et al., 2020), and deficiency of Kv9.3 disrupts parvalbumin interneuron physiology in mouse prefrontal cortex (Miyamae et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Deficiency of Kv9.3 disrupts parvalbumin interneuron physiology in mouse prefrontal cortex.
source: Kv5.1/Kv2.1 heteromers play an important role in controlling the excitability of mouse urinary bladder smooth muscle (Malysz and Petkov, 2020), mutations in Kv6.4 have been shown to influence human labor pain (Lee et al., 2020), and deficiency of Kv9.3 disrupts parvalbumin interneuron physiology in mouse prefrontal cortex (Miyamae et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miyamae et al., 2021.

claim: Deep sequencing has identified mRNA transcripts for Kcng2 (Kv6.2), Kcng3 (Kv6.3), Kcnv1 (Kv8.1) and Kcns3 (Kv9.3) present in GFP+ neurons from CalcaGFP mice.
source: Deep sequencing has identified mRNA transcripts for Kcng2 (Kv6.2), Kcng3 (Kv6.3), Kcnv1 (Kv8.1) and Kcns3 (Kv9.3) present in GFP+ neurons, an overlapping but distinct set of KvS subunits from the MrgprdGFP non-peptidergic population (Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2019.

claim: Kv5.1, Kv6.3, and Kv9.1 all slow deactivation of Kv2 conductances in heterologous cells.
source: Kv5.1, Kv6.3, and Kv9.1 all slow deactivation of Kv2 conductances in heterologous cells (Salinas et al., 1997b; Kramer et al., 1998; Sano et al., 2002), and in Kv2.1-CHO cells transfected with Kv5.1, we confirmed that RY785-resistant currents deactivate slower than Kv2.1 controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Salinas et al., 1997b, Kramer et al., 1998, and Sano et al., 2002.

claim: In Kv2.1-CHO cells transfected with Kv5.1, RY785-resistant currents deactivate slower than Kv2.1 controls.
source: Kv5.1, Kv6.3, and Kv9.1 all slow deactivation of Kv2 conductances in heterologous cells (Salinas et al., 1997b; Kramer et al., 1998; Sano et al., 2002), and in Kv2.1-CHO cells transfected with Kv5.1, we confirmed that RY785-resistant currents deactivate slower than Kv2.1 controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: RY785 is much less potent against other non-Kv2 voltage-gated potassium channel subfamilies as well as voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels.
source: However, we think RY785 is unlikely to have substantial off-target effects, as RY785 is much less potent against other non-Kv2 voltage-gated potassium channel subfamilies as well as voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels (Herrington et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herrington et al., 2011.

claim: Some KvS subunits are reported to functionally interact with Kv7 subunits.
source: Intriguingly, some KvS subunits are reported to functionally interact with Kv7 subunits (Renigunta et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Renigunta et al., 2024.
